author: livingstaccato
body:
Found while investigating a report of browsers misbehaving after a cache clear. Two profiles on the reporting machine held Chromium locks naming **long-dead pids whose sockets no longer existed**.

## The failure

Chromium marks a user-data-dir as in-use with three symlinks: `SingletonLock` → `<hostname>-<pid>`, `SingletonSocket` → a path in the OS temp dir, and `SingletonCookie`. If the browser dies without an orderly shutdown they survive — and on macOS the socket lives under `/var/folders/.../T/`, so a routine cache/temp sweep deletes it while the profile keeps the dangling lock.

Every later launch of that profile then fails:

```
BrowserType.launch_persistent_context: Opening in existing browser session.
This usually means that the profile is already in use by another instance of Chromium.
```

…and stays broken until someone deletes the files by hand. A persistent profile is what holds a persona's saved logins, so an unrelated temp cleanup silently bricks exactly the state users most want preserved.

## The fix

The launch path prunes such a lock before opening the context.

Conservative by design, because removing a **live** lock is worse than leaving a stale one — two Chromiums sharing a profile corrupt it. A lock is removed only when it names a pid **on this host** that is confirmed not running. Left alone in every other case:

| Case | Why |
|---|---|
| Live pid | The lock is doing its job |
| `PermissionError` on the pid | Running, owned by another user |
| Different hostname | Profile may be genuinely open on another machine (shared storage) |
| Unparsable target | Can't prove it's dead, so don't touch it |

Pruning never raises — a profile that can't be tidied is still attempted, so the user sees Chromium's own error rather than ours.

## Tests

Both directions: dead-owner and cleared-socket cases prune; live-owner, foreign-host, unparsable-target, no-lock and missing-dir cases don't. Plus an end-to-end check that a profile deliberately bricked with a dead-pid lock launches cleanly through `BrowserPool.launch` — verified against real Chromium before committing.

author: alex-feel
body:
Release-gate round 1 over v7.2.0..main confirmed four findings (dual-skeptic verified, one with a 10k-case fuzz):

1. **Alt+y silent decline (minor)**: the `ESC-any` catch-all consumed the character following a lone ESC, so `ESC y` (Alt+y in many terminals, or a truncated query reply adjacent to the answer) sanitized to `''` -- which `confirm_installation` treats as immediate deny, bypassing the re-prompt safety net. The pattern now strips any remaining bare ESC byte ALONE: Alt+y reduces to `y`, and stray residue characters hit the re-prompt instead of a silent misread.
2. **SS3 partial strip (advisory)**: `ESC O P` (xterm F1-F4) lost only two of three bytes, gluing the function-key identifier onto the answer. A dedicated SS3 branch now strips the sequence whole.
3. **Windows msvcrt drain untested (advisory)**: the win32 flush branch gains mocked tests (drain loop termination + missing-module silence).
4. **pty helper kill race (minor)**: timeout-path `os.kill` calls are now guarded so a child exiting exactly at the deadline cannot replace the informative timeout failure with a `ProcessLookupError` traceback.

Full suite: 3007 passed / 53 platform-skipped (pty suite re-verified on Linux via WSL); pre-commit clean.

author: fletcherreaves-cloud
body:
Closes #140.

## What this is — and isn't

The ack mechanism already existed and was already Supabase-persisted: `SwingAlarm.js` + `engine/swing-feed.js` (`ackKey`/`acknowledge`/`pruneAcks`, 120-day expiry), wired at `App.js` (swing_acks), and `AttentionPanel` (analytics.js) using the same machinery under a deliberately separate key (`attention_acks` — see the "Trap 2" comment in `swing-feed.js`: sharing one blob would let one feed's `pruneAcks` silently drop the other's acks). None of that was rebuilt.

The actual gap, per the issue: once acknowledged, an item disappeared with no way to see what was cleared, by whom, or when.

## What changed

**New: `buildAckHistory()`** in `swing-feed.js` — one merged, sorted (most-recent-first) list built by reading **both raw acks blobs directly**, not by cross-referencing against what's still live first. That's deliberate: an ack whose finding has since resolved and dropped off the live feed still shows up (`resolved:true`) until `pruneAcks` ages it out at 120 days — unchanged aging, now answerable instead of a surprise.

- **Swing acks**: the key (`${loc}:${week}:${severity}`) is always parseable — one stable producer, one shape — so a resolved swing ack still gets a real description built from the key itself.
- **Attention acks**: keys are opaque per-detector ids (`finding-${loc}-${rule}`, `fob-${loc}`, `stale`, ...) with no single safely-parseable shape across every detector. A resolved attention ack falls back to showing the **raw id**, not a guessed store — misattributing an old ack to the wrong store would be exactly the kind of surprise this feature exists to remove, not reintroduce.

`App.js` passes its already-loaded `swingAcks`/`swingItems` down to `AttentionPanel` (no duplicate load, no duplicate `buildSwingFeed` computation). `AttentionPanel`'s existing (already-near-top) Acknowledged section now renders the merged history — store, what, who, when — instead of only its own `attention_acks` partitioned against the live feed; the chip count and section header reflect the combined total.

**Explicitly did not touch**, per the issue: the situation key on either domain (an escalating store still surfaces as new), or `pruneAcks`' 120-day window.

## Verification

- **7 new tests** on `buildAckHistory`: empty case, merge across both sources, sort order, live-item enrichment for both domains, resolved-fallback for both domains, and the never-guess-a-store-from-an-opaque-id case for attention acks.
- `npm test`: **95 files / 1172 tests pass** (1165 + 7 new).
- `npm run build`: clean.
- **Unauthenticated boot-and-render pass** in a real Chromium, using the recipe from `memory/feedback-verification-in-sandbox.md` (committed today, `--no-proxy-server` + explicit `executablePath` — the fix for a Chromium/proxy issue that blocked me on the prior PR): app boots clean, full nav renders including **Needs Attention**, zero console errors. **What still needs the owner**: opening the panel itself and confirming the merged Acknowledged section renders correctly with real data — Supabase CORS blocks that from this sandbox (documented, genuine limit, not something a browser flag fixes).
- Entry chunk, measured against a fresh `main` baseline in an isolated worktree: **2726.22 KB → 2728.15 KB gzip 818.79 KB → 819.47 KB (+0.68 KB gzip)**.

## Process note

Draft PR per standing instruction — not merging. Owner/PM to review and merge.

author: groeneai
body:
<!--
Linked issues and pull requests.
-->

Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111799


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Documentation (changelog entry is not required)


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Documentation only.

### Description

Adds a `Data durability on power loss` section to the `Kafka`, `NATS` and `FileLog` engine documentation, at the request of the component owner on #111799. `S3Queue`/`AzureQueue` (#111571) and `RabbitMQ` (#111833) already document this; these three did not mention it.

`Kafka` and `NATS` commit the consumed position after the insert into the target, but nothing in the streaming path fsyncs the target part (`fsync_after_insert = 0` by default). If the OS page cache is lost between the commit and the fsync, the already-consumed rows are gone with no error and `count()` is simply smaller. Their notes follow the merged `RabbitMQ` wording and keep its scope limits: every target `MergeTree` needs the setting including cascaded materialized-view targets, asynchronous intermediaries need their own, and paths that commit before the insert finishes are not covered (`kafka_commit_every_batch` only on the broker-backed engine, since it is ignored when `kafka_keeper_path` is set). The `NATS` note is scoped to JetStream, since core NATS has no acknowledgements and is already documented as at-most-once.

`FileLog` gets a deliberately different note, because its ordering is inverted: it records the consumed offset from inside the reading pipeline, before the insert that chunk belongs to is committed. An ordinary process failure is therefore enough to leave the recorded offset ahead of the data that reached the target, and the rows are skipped on restart with no power loss involved. For the same reason `fsync_after_insert = 1` on the target cannot close the window, so the note documents that limitation and the practical mitigation instead of recommending the setting.

The text goes in the engines' embedded `DOCS_MD` blocks, the single source the rendered pages are generated from; the `.mdx` generated regions belong to the nightly job and are untouched. Verified via `system.table_engines`: the three descriptions gain the section, the three already-documented engines are byte-identical.

author: akz142857
body:
## 现象

`模型部署` 页面上，一个部署的价格列已经显示「已设置」，下方却仍挂着红色的「无法完成请求 — 该部署没有已生效的价格版本」。刷新页面才消失。

## 原因

那条横幅不是从部署状态推导出来的，它是**启用**这个 mutation 失败后留下的错误对象（`deployment_price_unavailable`），渲染在 `DeploymentsPage.tsx` 的 `ErrorState` 里。点「设置价格」成功后只失效了 `deployment-prices` 查询——价格列因此翻成「已设置」，但那个死掉的 mutation 从没被 reset，于是同一行里两个控件互相矛盾。

## 修复

部署一旦拥有 active 价格版本，就清掉这个错误（顺带让重试从干净的 mutation 状态开始）。只安排了未来生效、当前没有 active 版本的情况保留横幅——那种情况下启用确实仍会被拒绝，横幅是对的。

## 验证

- 新增回归测试 `clears the missing-price blocker once the price it demanded exists`，走完整流程：启用被拒 → 横幅出现 → 设置价格 → 横幅消失。
- 反向验证：把修复注释掉后该测试失败，且失败点正是「横幅应消失」这一断言——价格列已翻成「已设置」的那行断言先通过了，复现了截图里的矛盾状态。
- `npm run typecheck` 干净；前端全量 280 tests / 32 files 通过。

body:
## Cierre de perfiles y self-service del conductor

### Autoridad
- El rol persistente canónico sigue siendo `driver`; `conductor` queda sólo como alias de compatibilidad en contratos legacy.
- El conductor conserva autoridad sobre nombre, correo, teléfono, foto, contraseña y claves E2EE mediante `PATCH /users/me`.
- Administración conserva horario operativo, turno, asignación/liberación de unidad y acciones explícitas de baja/reactivación/eliminación.
- `PATCH /users/:userId` ya no puede sobrescribir identidad/credenciales/rol/estado de un driver por la vía genérica.

### UX
- Restaura `Mis documentos` como acción secundaria driver-only en Perfil.
- No vuelve la tarjeta grande eliminada en #125 y no expone Directorio al conductor.

body:
Hop two of two. Promotes `uat` → `main`, carrying **`#151`** — the board-pagination fix.

## What it fixes

`gh-board.ts` requested `items(first: 50)` with no `pageInfo` and no loop, so **`gov` read the first 50 board items and nothing else.**

Board `Svayamtech/projects/115` holds 103 items across three repositories; the CLI's own query returned 50 from **one**. Every command deriving repos from the board — `task`, `merge`, `sync` — silently operated on the workspace repo alone **while reporting success**. It skipped a present, correctly-branched repo three separate times during PRJ-115, each needing manual `git` to finish what the command claimed to have done.

Also carries the `gov-work` → `gov` rename completed in `src`/`test`/`e2e`: 44 user-facing invocations renamed, 67 package/product nouns deliberately left.

## Verification

- **620 tests** (617 + 3 new), `tsc` + `eslint` clean, on a branch cut from `dev`.
- **Against the live board after the fix:** `linkedItemCount: 101`, all three repos. Before: 50, one repo.
- Regression tests include a two-page board whose first page is entirely one repo — the shape that hid it. Raising the page size is not a fix; 100 is GraphQL's maximum, so the cliff only moves.
- Non-terminating paging **throws** rather than returning a partial board.

## After this merges

Reaching `main` fixes what `gov upgrade` serves, but **the truncation lives in the CLI, not the content** — every existing install keeps reading 50 items until `@svayam-opensource/gov` is republished. The release is the step that actually retires the bug.

author: shahbaz242630
body:
Slice 1.10e — the auth pages. Second of the three things left in the
2026-08-09 design package; only the landing page remains, and it is blocked.

## What is new

| Route | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `/sign-in`, `/sign-up` | Dressed in the split screen. Sign-in gains "Forgot your password?" |
| `/signed-out` | **New.** Where signing out lands now |
| `/reset-password` | **New.** Ask for the address, send the link |
| `/auth/confirm` | **New route handler.** Where every emailed link comes back to |
| `/new-password` | **New.** Where a recovery link lands, once it is a session |
| `/change-password` | **New.** Signed in, with re-authentication |

**Signing out used to land on `/sign-in`.** That is the identical screen a
failed session produces, so choosing to leave read as "that didn't work, try
again". `/signed-out` says the thing that actually matters at that moment:
reminders already scheduled still go out.

**"Forgot your password" was not a link to add — it was a flow to build.**
`/auth/confirm` is the whole reason: without it the emailed link has nowhere
to land, and the person who clicked it is stranded holding a token no page
will accept.

## The confirm route handles both token shapes, deliberately

Supabase's default recovery template comes back as `?code=` — a PKCE exchange
that only works in **the same browser that asked for the reset**, because the
verifier lives in that browser's cookie. Request it on a laptop, open the mail
on a phone, get nothing. The cross-device fix is a dashboard template change
to `?token_hash=…&type=recovery`, which `verifyOtp` accepts from anywhere.

Supporting both means the flow works **today** on the default template and
keeps working the moment the template is improved — no code change, and no
window where it is broken.

`next` arrives from an email and is treated as hostile: anything but a
single-slash-relative path is discarded, because `//evil.example` is a
protocol-relative URL browsers follow off-site. An open redirect would be one
careless `startsWith("/")` away, on the one link a customer is primed to click
without looking.

## The panels state no facts about a customer, and the prototype's did

The design draws **"14 reminders sent · 3 waiting"**, **"Second reminder ·
INV-2041"**, and a next scheduled run for a named firm. On a sign-in page
nobody is signed in, so a number in that position reads as *your* number —
invented, on the screen where a stranger is deciding whether this product
tells the truth. Same ruling as the testimonials: we have no customers, so
there is nothing true to put there.

Every line now describes how Eva behaves, which is true for everyone and needs
no session to say. **A test reads the source and fails if any of it comes
back** — and fails on a digit appearing in any panel at all, because a digit
is the shape the fabrications took.

Three more claims dropped for the same reason:

- **"No card needed"** — pricing is one of the four decisions still with the
  founder. We do not currently take a card, so it is probably true; probably
  true is not a standard for the page where somebody hands over their email.
- **"Back to eva.co.uk"** — we do not own it.
- **"Changing your password signs out your other devices"** — it may well be
  true, but nobody has checked, and someone reading it might reasonably decide
  *not* to go and sign out a lost phone.

## The routing rule is the part that fails silently for somebody else

Extracted as `routeKind` so a test can reach it. Every one of these routes
renders perfectly while you are signed out and looking at the signed-out case.
Put `/new-password` in the anonymous-only list by mistake and nothing looks
wrong — the recovery link just bounces to the dashboard for a real customer,
who never gets to set a password and has no idea why.

It is also why `/new-password` is **not** nested under `/reset-password`: as
`/reset-password/new` it would inherit anonymous-only and bounce the one
session it exists to serve. That trap is stated in a test so the next person
tidying the URLs meets it before their customers do.

## Mutation results

Seven mutations against the fourteen new tests; all seven failed the suite.

| Mutation | Caught by |
| --- | --- |
| recovery screen moved to the anonymous-only list | route-kind |
| confirm route swept into the protected list | route-kind |
| prefix matching loses its segment boundary | route-kind |
| change-password left open to anyone | route-kind |
| an invented activity figure returns to a panel | panel claims |
| an invented invoice number returns to a panel | panel claims |
| the charcoal panel stacks above the form on a phone | auth frame |

## ⚠️ Two Supabase dashboard settings this needs

Neither can be done from code, and the reset flow is **untested end to end
until the first is confirmed**:

1. **Redirect allowlist** must include `…/auth/confirm` for both origins —
   `https://web-production-15df9.up.railway.app` and
   `https://web-staging-4726.up.railway.app`. Without it the emailed link
   silently falls back to the Site URL and the customer lands on the home page
   with no way to set a password.
2. **Recommended, not required:** the recovery email template →
   `{{ .SiteURL }}/auth/confirm?token_hash={{ .TokenHash }}&type=recovery&next=/new-password`,
   which makes the link work on a different device from the one that asked.
   The code already accepts it.

Also worth turning on while in there: **Secure password change**, which makes
Supabase itself require a recent sign-in. Our current-password field is
re-authentication we perform ourselves; that setting is the real one.

## Gate

1267 tests (api 708, db 176, web 365, worker 18) — was 1253. Build, lint,
typecheck and `format:check` clean, from a freshly recreated `eva_test`.

## Not proven

**No password has actually been reset.** The screens were verified by
rendering the real components against the real compiled stylesheet; the flow
itself needs a live run with a real inbox, and that run is the next thing to
do once the redirect allowlist above is confirmed.

author: jlucaso1
body:
## Summary

`decodeProto` threw for any 64-bit field whose value fell outside ±(2^53−1):

```
Error: Value is larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
```

The damage was never the one field. The throw escapes the whole `decode()` call, so a legitimate server payload — a large `fileLength`, a microsecond timestamp, a 64-bit id — cost the consumer the entire message: url, mimetype, caption, media key, everything.

**Before:** an in-range 64-bit field decoded to `number`; an out-of-range one threw and took the message with it.
**After:** an in-range 64-bit field decodes to the *identical* `number`; an out-of-range one decodes to the protobufjs `Long` split `{ low, high, unsigned }`, exact to all 64 bits, and the rest of the message arrives intact.

This is a breaking change at the type level only — see below.

## Reproduction

`tests/proto-int64-range.test.ts`, added in dd6aa45 before any fix. Pure codec: no wasm, no client, no network.

The boundary is exactly where the report said it was. `bun run` against `ts/proto.ts` on `main`:

```
9007199254740991 -> {"videoMessage":{"url":"https://x","fileLength":9007199254740991,"seconds":12}}
9007199254740992 -> THROWS: Value is larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
```

`bun test tests/proto-int64-range.test.ts` at dd6aa45 — 8 fail, 4 pass (the 4 that pass are the in-range and `2^53−1` cases, which are there to pin the non-regression):

```
(fail) decodes an unsafe uint64 instead of failing the message
(fail) decodes an unsafe negative int64 instead of failing the message
(fail) carries the rest of the message across untouched
(fail) pins the uint64 boundary at max+1
(fail) pins the int64 boundary at max+1
(fail) pins the int64 boundary at min-1
(fail) re-encodes what it decoded to the same bytes
(fail) keeps a message carrying an unsafe field JSON-serializable
 4 pass
 8 fail
```

Both edges are pinned in the tests, for both signednesses: `9007199254740991` / `9007199254740992` and `-9007199254740991` / `-9007199254740992`, plus `u64::MAX` and `i64::MIN`. `tests/proto-reader.test.ts` pins the same boundary one level down, per reader method, including `sint64`/`fixed64`/`sfixed64`.

## Root cause

The ceiling is not in Rust and not in ts-proto's schema — it is this repo's own output contract, and it was deliberate.

`scripts/gen-ts-proto.ts` post-processes the ts-proto output so every `longToNumber(reader.uint64())` becomes `reader.uint64Number()`, a method on the `BinaryReader` subclass in `ts/proto-reader.ts`. That subclass exists for a real reason: Buf's own `uint64()` materializes a BigInt and then a decimal string on the way to a number, and `positiveSafeVarint()` avoids even allocating Buf's `[low, high]` tuple for the common value. The `…Number()` names were the tell — the reader was written to return `number`, and the ceiling was the direct consequence:

```ts
const assertSafeInteger = (value: number): number => {
  if (value > Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) throw new Error("Value is larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER");
  if (value < Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER) throw new Error("Value is smaller than Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER");
  return value;
};
```

`AGENTS.md` documented it as intentional ("ts-proto is configured to expose every 64-bit field as a `number` and to reject unsafe values … on purpose"). No finer-grained history exists — `ts/proto-reader.ts` and `scripts/gen-ts-proto.ts` both trace to the single `feat: major rewrite` commit — so the recorded intent is that AGENTS.md line and the code itself.

**The reason worth preserving is the fast path, not the throw.** Nothing in the performance argument requires *rejecting* the wide value; the throw was the cheapest way to keep the return type `number`. That has been preserved (numbers below), and only the rejection is gone. `AGENTS.md` is updated in this PR so it no longer describes a contract the code has left.

One correction to the pre-research: the emitted types declared `number`, not `Long`/`bigint`/`string` — e.g. `messageTimestamp?: number | undefined`. That is what makes this a type break.

## Design

Four options, weighed by what a consumer already on 0.7.2 actually suffers:

| | `JSON.stringify(msg)` | `x > 1000` | `x + 1` | `String(x)` | re-encode |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `number \| bigint` | **throws — whole message** | correct | **throws** | correct | ok |
| `number \| string` | ok | coerced, precision lost at the margin | silent concat | correct | ok |
| `number \| Long` | ok | `false` (NaN) | NaN | `[object Object]` | ok |
| saturate to `number` | ok | plausible but wrong | plausible but wrong | plausible but wrong | wrong bytes |

- **Always `bigint`** — rejected. It breaks every consumer, and `JSON.stringify` refuses BigInt, which reproduces the exact bug being fixed one layer up: one wide field takes down the serialization of the whole message. This repo has already hit that twice and written it down twice (`camel_serializer.rs`, `wasm_utils.rs`).
- **Always `string`** — rejected. Also breaks every consumer, including the ~100% of values that fit fine today, and `"9007199254740993" + 1` is silently wrong.
- **Saturate / truncate to `number`** — rejected. It discards exactness with no signal at all, and it breaks the round-trip: the re-encoded bytes differ from the ones received. That is strictly worse than the current throw, which at least fails loudly.
- **`number` when it fits, `Long` when it does not** — chosen.

Why `Long` and not `bigint` for the wide case: `{ low, high, unsigned }` is not a new representation invented here. `src/camel_serializer.rs` already emits exactly this shape for *every* i64/u64 on the event path, `encodeProto` already accepts it (`normalizeProtoInput`, covered by `tests/proto-quoted-long.test.ts`), and `AGENTS.md` already documents it. A consumer that reads message events already has the handling. Choosing `bigint` or `string` here would have made three representations of a 64-bit integer inside one package.

The union does cost the consumer a narrowing check, and a consumer doing arithmetic straight on a 64-bit field will now get `NaN` on large values rather than a number. That is the price of the option that does not break the common case — and `NaN` beats `string` concatenation or a saturated value, both of which look like answers.

**No flag / separate entrypoint.** A flag would leave the default behaviour "lose the message", which nobody would deliberately opt into, and it would fork the codec's hot path. The runtime behaviour here is a strict superset: every input that produced a value before produces the identical value now; only inputs that used to *throw* behave differently. The type change is the honest signal, so it ships as the default.

### What changed

- `ts/proto-reader.ts` — `Long` / `Int64` exported; `assertSafeInteger` replaced by `unsignedWordsToInt64` / `signedWordsToInt64`; `positiveSafeVarint()` rewinds to the two-word path instead of throwing; `*Number()` → `*Value()`, because the old name asserted a contract that no longer holds.
- `ts/proto-reader.ts` — `BinaryWriter` is now a subclass that takes `Long` back on the five 64-bit setters. Buf's setters accept `number | bigint | string`, so a decoded `Long` handed straight to `Message.encode()` would have reached `BigInt(object)` and thrown.
- `scripts/gen-ts-proto.ts` — retypes the 212 64-bit interface members from `number` to `Int64`. Which members those are is only visible in each message's decode block, so the script collects them there and rewrites the matching interface fields, erroring if a read has no matching member or a read appears in an unhandled shape. Also drops ts-proto's now-dead `longToNumber`, so the file no longer carries a helper whose thrown errors read like the codec's contract.
- `scripts/gen-protobufjs-dts.ts` — the public `proto-types` surface renders those fields as `Long`, and the header's `type Long = number` stub (previously dead) becomes the real union.
- `ts/index.ts` — `Int64`, `Long` and `longToBigInt` ar

author: justinhandley
body:
Mirrors `nestled-dev-template@e2fdec0`. Seventeen files.

**Refreshed** after nestledjs/nestled-dev-template#89 merged, so this no longer carries the broken JWT decode that review of the first cut found. Re-mirrored from scratch rather than patched on top, so this is one clean commit.

## The bump is the important part

`@nestledjs/access-control` moves `^0.0.1` → `^0.0.2`, and this is not routine: **`0.0.1` ships development-only JSX that crashes in production.** Any downstream already consuming `0.0.1` is carrying a production fault. The note's agentHints say so outright, so the bump doesn't read as cosmetic and get deferred.

## What lands

| Note | What it fixes |
| --- | --- |
| `2026-08-10-access-control-production-jsx` | the crash above |
| `2026-08-10-browser-safe-jwt-decode` | duplicate-cookie selection was silently inert in the browser |
| `2026-08-10-duplicate-session-cookie-auth` | picks the **newest** session cookie rather than the first match |
| `2026-08-10-auth-error-navigation` | preserves the complete return route through an auth error |

Plus `apps/web/app/access-denied.tsx`, replacing a client-side redirect to `/force-logout`.

## Why the JWT fix exists, and why it was fixed upstream

The duplicate-cookie selection decoded tokens through `Buffer` — which no browser provides and this bundle does not polyfill — so on the client it threw for **every** token. The throw landed inside the `catch` that skips malformed tokens, leaving the positional fallback as the normal path. `document.cookie` orders by path specificity rather than age, so that fallback returns the **stale** token in precisely the case the feature exists to handle. Silently, with a green suite: the only coverage exercised the SSR request-header path, where `Buffer` exists.

Fixed in dev-template, not here, because this file is mirrored — a direct edit would be reverted by the next promotion. This mirror carries the corrected decoder, its guards, and the warning that makes the fallback audible.

## This also reconciles a divergence worth flagging

Scoped RBAC was committed **directly to this repo** in `57f6184` and `e067044` rather than flowing down from dev-template. The promotion contract forbids that precisely because the mirror overwrites — anything living only here is silently replaced.

Nothing was lost this time: dev-template held those same commits *plus* the later fixes, and I checked every non-lockfile deletion individually — all are in-place rewrites, not dropped work. But that was luck, and the JWT decoder above is the argument for the rule: it was found in review *here* and could only be fixed *there*.

## Verification

- `nx test apollo` **17 passed**, `nx test web` **709 passed**
- 80 upgrade notes validate
- No new "Template-only" entries, so nothing upstream was deleted needing hand-removal

One expected artifact: a dry-run will always report `apps/web/package.json` as pending. That is the imported-vs-embedded seam — dev-template uses `workspace:*`, this repo consumes the published `^0.0.2` — rewritten every run. Not incompleteness.

author: novanglus96
body:
My cutover stub said `image_list: app`. This repo's `docker-compose-prod.yml` builds **frontend, backend and worker** (`lenoreschedule_frontend`/`_backend`/`_worker`) at both `v0.0.1` and `main` — there is no `app` service on any release branch.

## How it surfaced

The backfill build failed with `KeyError: 'app'`. That is the reusable workflow behaving **correctly**: it reads the real image name out of `docker compose config` rather than assuming one, so a service name that does not exist cannot silently resolve to an empty string and publish garbage. (The old `build_publish.yml` did the opposite — see the `":production" is not a valid repository/tag` failure that `docker_tag_check` hid.)

## Cause, because it is a trap rather than a typo

The shape survey was run against the **working tree** while this checkout was still on a feature branch (`fix/pdf-italic-unconfirmed`) carrying the single-container refactor. `main` does not have it. Read shapes from `git show <ref>:<path>`, never the working tree — a stale local checkout caused confusion during LenoreFin's cutover too.

Docker Hub agrees: `lenoreschedule_frontend` and `_backend` exist, `lenoreschedule_worker` does **not** (404) — because publish here has never once worked, thanks to the `$GITHUB_ENV` typo. The backfill will create it.

author: hsaab
body: ## Summary Sets up a Cloud Agent development environment for this Vite + React 19 SPA by adding a repository-managed `.cursor/environment.json`. No application code is touched, and all keynote demo safety nets remain intact. The config: - `install`: `npm ci` — clean, lockfile-faithful dependency install - `terminals.dev`: `npm run dev` — the Vite dev server (visible logs, restartable) - `ports`: `5173` — forwards the dev server ## Why this shape This is a pure client-side SPA (no backend, no database, no Docker). The default Cloud Agent base image already provides Node 22 / npm 10, so no custom Dockerfile is needed. Dependency install belongs in `install`; the long-running dev server belongs in `terminals` so its logs stay visible and it can be restarted. There is no per-boot daemon to reconcile, so `start` is unused. author: lenzo-ka
body:
Makes collections answerable: structural queries over stored forms, and a derivation predicate that says whether one form was derived from another under a grammar — with a witness or an honest refusal.

## Structural query (`ipakit/_corpus_query.py`)

`query(corpus, pattern, role=...)` streams (fileid, match sites) over a collection, restoring only the queried role, one entry at a time — first match after a single restoration, memory bounded by matches rather than corpus size. Patterns are the rewrite engine's own recognize half: a query string is the rule notation without the arrow (`[vowel] / _ [nasal]`, `t / [vowel] _ #`), compiled into the engine's `Pattern`/`Query` objects — the sites a query returns are identical to the sites the corresponding rule would fire at, including margins, virtual edges, and stress-on-nucleus. Agreement variables are bind-only in queries: `n / _ [place=α]` matches and carries `α`'s bound value on each site, and one variable still cannot range over two feature domains — with or without an environment. Zero targets (`∅`, `[zero]`, `0`, `Ø`) are refused at parse: an insertion site is not a recognizable pattern. Match sites are canonical graph paths, correct under reindexing (boundaries, marks, rewrite-projected and epenthesis-projected forms).

## Derivation checking

`derives(ruleset, source, target)` answers "was this derived from that" three ways, never as a bare boolean:

- a witness `Derivation` — the fired rules, sites, and layers, replayable to the target;
- `ExhaustiveRefusal` — no witness, and the variants space was fully explored;
- `BudgetRefusal` — no witness found, with the count of unexplored combinations under the branching cap.

Deterministic grammars short-circuit to run-and-compare. `query_derivations` maps the predicate over a collection's (source, target) role pairs, streaming per-entry answers — the induction fitness scorer and the invertibility-report engine. All eight attested gairaigo pairs return replay-verified witnesses under `japanese-moraic`.

Role-selective restoration lands in the corpus kernel (`read_roles`), so querying never restores what it does not read.

All shipped-output gates byte-identical; `make check` green.

author: galeote
body:
Los dos huecos del SDK que destapó el **primer integrador real** al reconstruir
su puente sobre `external_ref` (`pimia-puente-compai`, Fase 1). Ambos son
**aditivos**: ninguna llamada existente cambia de firma ni de comportamiento.

## 1. `convertToInvoice()` no podía mandar la referencia

El endpoint acepta `external_ref` en el cuerpo desde la 0.4.0 — y no es un
extra: es lo que hace que `invoice.created` e `invoice.paid` lleguen con la
referencia del integrador en vez de con `null`. **Tiene que ir en la
conversión**; etiquetar después con `PUT /invoices/{id}` llega tarde, porque
para entonces `invoice.created` ya salió nulo y entre las dos llamadas hay una
ventana en la que la factura existe y no se encuentra por su referencia.

El atajo no tenía por dónde mandarlo (`convertToInvoice(id, options)`), así que
el integrador tuvo que bajar a `pimia.post()` crudo — es decir, el helper dejaba
de servir justo en el paso que cierra el bucle, que es para lo que existe.

```ts
await client.estimates.convertToInvoice(55, {
  externalRef: 'deal:42',
  idempotencyKey: 'deal:42:invoice',
})
```

Va como **opción** y no como segundo parámetro para no romperle la llamada a
quien ya hace `convertToInvoice(id, { idempotencyKey })` — con una firma
`(id, body, options)` ese objeto se habría enviado como cuerpo. `external_ref`
es además el único campo que el endpoint acepta, así que el atajo puede montar
el cuerpo él. Un `externalRef: null` explícito **desvincula** la referencia;
omitirlo manda cuerpo vacío, exactamente como hasta ahora.

## 2. No se podía poner un timeout a una lectura

`get(path, query)` y `delete(path)` no aceptaban opciones, ni tampoco los seis
atajos de recurso (`customers.list/get`, `estimates.list/get`,
`invoices.list/get`). Para pasar un `AbortSignal` había que abandonar los atajos
e irse a `request()`.

Y en la práctica nadie se va: se queda sin timeout. El puente lo documentó así
—«un `await` que nunca vuelve tampoco llega al `finally`»— y es el peor modo de
fallo que hay, porque un cliente que sondea deja de sondear **sin dar un solo
error**. Entra `ReadOptions` (`headers`, `signal`), exportado desde el índice.

```ts
await client.get('/currencies', undefined, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20_000) })
await client.customers.get(7, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20_000) })
```

## Verificación

**55/55 tests** (48 previos intactos + 7 nuevos) y `typecheck` limpio. Los
nuevos fijan: que la señal llega al `fetch` en `get`, `delete` y los atajos; que
la query sigue funcionando y que un `undefined` no se cuela en la URL; que
`convertToInvoice` manda `{external_ref}` sin filtrar la opción a las cabeceras;
que sin `externalRef` el cuerpo sigue siendo `{}`; y que el `null` explícito se
distingue de la omisión.

## Lo que NO toca, y hay que decidir

**El SDK PHP.** No tiene helper de `convertToInvoice`, y su equivalente del
timeout es una opción del cliente HTTP, no un `AbortSignal`, así que el hueco no
es el mismo. Pero este monorepo **versiona en bloque**, así que conviene decidir
si la paridad entra en la misma release o se declara explícitamente que el atajo
de convert es solo de TypeScript.

**La versión.** Añado la entrada en `[Sin publicar]` del CHANGELOG y no toco
`package.json`: por el precedente de las tres releases anteriores, el bump y el
tag los hace el release, no el PR de la función. Por SemVer 0.x esto es una
minor (0.5.0): añade superficie pública.

author: pinefruitdev
body:
`VerseCode/DeviceTemplate/my_device.verse` had drifted far enough from Core that following it would not compile. None of Device1 through Device4 use the shape it describes, so anyone starting from the template hits errors immediately and has to reverse engineer a shipped device instead.

What was wrong:

- `Logger` was called as `Logger().Print("...")`. The real signature on `base_device` is `Logger(Message : string, ?Name : string = "")`.
- The class was wrapped in `my_device_module := module:`. No shipped device does this. Modules come from the folder plus `module_access.verse`, so the class belongs at file scope.
- `using { Core }` was missing, and the parent was written as `base_group_device` rather than `Core.base_group_device`.
- Tooltips used an inline `@tooltip("...")`. Shipped devices declare a localized message at file scope and reference it as `@editable { ToolTip := SomeTip }`.
- `LOGGER_NAME` was never overridden, so every line a new device logged would say "Base Device".
- `OnAgentRespawned` had a comment and no body, which is not a valid block.
- The lifecycle comments described joining a *group*. These hooks fire on joining the island. That is a misleading first impression of the Core for exactly the audience the template exists to serve.

The README's setup steps also still told people to update a module declaration that no longer exists, so they point at `module_access.verse` now, and the dependency list mentions `utility.verse`.

I kept `base_group_device` as the parent so this stays a fix rather than a redesign, with a note pointing at `base_device` for devices that need no groups. Happy to flip the default if you would rather the template start groupless, since that is probably the more common case.

Not compiled. Verse only builds in UEFN, so this needs a pass through the editor before it is trusted.

body:
## C.3A — Shadow Migration da Contratação Direta para o Kernel Cognitivo

Primeira migração supervisionada do plano (`AI_LEGACY_MIGRATION_PLAN §4.1`), **EXCLUSIVAMENTE SHADOW**. O legado permanece **EFFECTIVE** (resposta oficial); o Kernel canônico roda em paralelo só para medir equivalência. **Sem cutover · sem migration · sem alterar allowlists/freeze · flag default OFF.**

> **Graphify:** consultado → confirmado no código → atualizado ao final (novo serviço/domínio/rota).

### Fluxo legado (inalterado)
UI → `directContracts.generate.{termoDispensa|termoInexigibilidade|minutaContrato|planilhaCotacao|mapaComparativo}` → `directContractDocuments.ts` (`invokeLLM` legado) → persiste → retorna `{documentId, content}`. **Contrato público byte-a-byte inalterado.**

### Fluxo shadow
`directContractsRouter` (após gerar+persistir legado) → `fireDirectContractShadow` **fire-and-forget** → `directContractShadowService` → `executeCognitiveTask({task:"DIRECT_PROCUREMENT_REASONING", businessDomain:"contratacao_direta"})`. Resultado shadow **não** volta ao usuário, **não** persiste documento, **não** altera status/workflow, **não** aparece na UI.

### Feature flag
`FF_DIRECT_CONTRACT_SHADOW` via `isFeatureEnabled(flag, organizationId)` (`featureFlagService`, DB, **tenant-aware**, **default OFF/fail-closed**). OFF ⇒ comportamento = legado puro. Sem seed/rollout%/hardcode.

### Replay safety
`runWithIdempotency` (único), chave `dc-shadow:{org}:{directContractId}:{docType}:{sha256(input)}`. Replay não reexecuta nem duplica observabilidade; payload diferente → chave diferente.

### Comparação (estrutural, não jurídica)
`compareDirectContractShadow` (puro, determinístico): `EQUIVALENT_STRUCTURE` · `STRUCTURAL_DIVERGENCE` · `MISSING_REQUIRED_FIELD` · `CANONICAL_ERROR` · `LEGACY_ERROR` · `NOT_COMPARABLE`. Sem julgamento "juridicamente correto/aprovado".

### Observabilidade (reuso, sem migration)
`cognitive_observability`: `executeCognitiveTask` grava a linha canônica; a comparação persiste via `insertObservability` (`payload.shadowComparison` = classificação, divergência, legacyHash, canonicalHash, provider/model, durações, sinais estruturais). **Sem chain-of-thought, sem conteúdo integral.**

### Isolamento de falhas / multi-tenant
`runDirectContractShadow` nunca lança; falha do canônico/observabilidade fica observável e **não derruba o legado**. `organizationId` explícito em flag/idempotência/observabilidade; flag por tenant; isolamento coberto no smoke.

### Boundaries preservadas
`INVOKE_LLM_LEGACY_ALLOWLIST` / `AI_SDK_ALLOWLIST` / `LEGACY_ACTIVE_MAINTENANCE_ONLY` **intactas**; `directContractDocuments`/`invokeLLM` não removidos; **nenhum novo consumidor de `invokeLLM`** (caminho novo usa `executeCognitiveTask`). `rc352`/`rc41`/legacy-freeze verdes.

### Migration
**Nenhuma** (reuso de `cognitive_observability` + `feature_flags`/`tenant_feature_flags`).

### Testes e gates (head `037c404`)
- `pnpm check` ✅ · lint `--max-warnings 0` ✅ · `pnpm test` **4589/166 skip** ✅ · `pnpm build` ✅ · `audit:gate` ✅ · rc352/rc41/legacy-freeze/migrations-chain ✅.
- Novos: `direct-contract-shadow` (unit) + `direct-contract-shadow-mysql-smoke` (CI: flag ON/OFF, observabilidade, replay, multi-tenant) + step no `ci.yml`.

### Rollback
Desligar `FF_DIRECT_CONTRACT_SHADOW` → shadow para; nada mais a reverter.

### Fora de escopo
Cutover · shadow na UI · migração de `legalFrameworkAssistant`/`legalOpinionService`/`catmatMatcher`/`gemini` · remoção de legado · `minScore` CATMAT · Railway/secrets/flags de produção.

author: frankbria
body:
Closes #1114.

## Two modes, because they are not equivalent

| flag | how it answers | survives a rejection? |
|---|---|---|
| `--brief-file <path>` | reads each question and answers *that* question from a project brief | **yes** |
| `--answers-file <path>` | JSON array consumed in order | **no** |

That distinction is the whole issue, and it is why shipping only `--answers-file`
would not have closed it.

## I reproduced the failure the issue describes

The report measured a canned list at **21 turns, 0 accepted, coverage stuck at
0%**. I hit exactly that against a live model with `--answers-file` — five
substantive, on-topic answers, one rejected as addressing a different question,
and the run ended stranded:

```
Error: --answers-file ran out of answers after 5 of 5.
Discovery was still on question 2 at 67% coverage.
The questions are AI-generated, so a fixed list can desynchronise if an answer
is rejected. Add more answers, or run interactively to finish the session.
```

`--brief-file`, same brief, same model:

```
✓ PRD generated: Self-Hosted Todo Management REST API
real  1m6.749s          exit 0, no TTY
```

**A complete PRD without a TTY** — AC #1 actually satisfied, not satisfied on
paper.

## The retry cap is part of the same change, not a nice-to-have

Without it, `--answers-file` reproduces the original hang with **no TTY to
interrupt it** — strictly worse than the interactive version. `MAX_ANSWER_ATTEMPTS
= 5`:

- **interactive** — says what is happening ("questions often have two parts"),
  and offers the `/pause` a stuck user would otherwise have to discover
- **non-interactive** — stops and explains that a canned list cannot resynchronise

## Loud exhaustion

Running out now raises `AnswersExhausted` and reports the question number and
coverage it stopped at. Before it was EOF inside `Prompt.ask` — an opaque
traceback naming neither.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] A non-interactive input source that produces a PRD without a TTY —
      `--brief-file`, verified end to end against a live model
- [x] Fails loudly and specifically when it runs out of answers
- [x] A retry cap per question that tells the user how to proceed
- [x] A test drives `cf prd generate` end to end without a TTY (no `input=`)
- [x] `scripts/quickstart-cleanroom/` **can** drop `responder.py` — see below

22 tests, including the always-rejecting-validator scenario asserting it
terminates instead of looping. `ruff` clean; `tests/cli/`: **574 passed**.

## Judgment calls

- **I did not delete `responder.py` in this PR.** The AC says the harness *can*
  drop it, and `--brief-file` is the supported replacement — it is the same idea
  in-process, minus 206 lines of pty/subprocess plumbing. But swapping the #614
  harness over changes what that walkthrough measures (a stand-in user driving
  the real CLI vs. the CLI answering itself), and #614 is someone's evidence
  artifact. That swap deserves its own change with the walkthrough re-run, rather
  than riding along here.
- **JSON array for `--answers-file`**, not one-per-line: real answers are prose
  and wrap. One format keeps the failure modes obvious.
- **`--brief-file` uses the standard provider resolution chain**, so
  `--llm-provider` / config apply to the stand-in answerer too.

## Known limitations

- `--answers-file` against a real model is unreliable **by nature**, not by
  defect. It is documented as such in `--help` and points at `--brief-file`. It
  remains the right choice for CI, where the provider is deterministic.
- `--brief-file` costs one extra LLM call per question. That is inherent to
  answering the question actually asked.

author: salatmaster
body:
Three changes to the `plugin.xml` description, which is what the Marketplace listing
shows.

**The first 40 characters.** [JetBrains puts them in preview cards](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/docs/marketplace/best-practices-for-listing.html).
Ours spent them on nothing:

```
before: 'Go semantic tools for the MCP server bui'
after:  'Your agent stops grepping Go and starts '
```

The README's opening line says the whole thing inside that budget, so it moves here.

**The interfaces bullet undersold 0.1.2.** Its strongest claim is not the
pointer-receiver trap but that a type declaring no method at all — the whole set gained
by embedding — is still found. That is precisely what no text search and no naive index
lookup can do, and it was the bug a user reported, so it belongs in the pitch rather
than only in the changelog.

**Requirements were missing**: the bundled MCP Server and Go plugins, and an agent
connected to the IDE. Someone reads the description before any instructions, and "it
does nothing after installing" is where that ends up otherwise.

Also "for the MCP server" → "added to the MCP server". This is not a server; it
contributes tools to one, which is the same distinction that keeps us out of MCP
registries.

Verified: `plugin.xml` parses, the description body is well-formed with only the tags it
already used, `verifyPluginStructure` passes, suite green. The listing itself only
changes on the next upload.

author: whusterj
body:
## Why

A malformed `depends-on` in an observer remedy commit reached `main` in a repository under observation, breaking `spekk validate` for everyone, and causing two scheduled agent runs to fail.

## What changed

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| builder | `spekk validate` before commit | unchanged |
| coach, writing assertions | `spekk list` / `spekk next` | plus `spekk validate` |
| coach, re-coordinating | "Validate with parser", **before** the edit | `spekk validate`, after it |
| coordinator skill | `parseAllSpecs()` | `spekk validate` |
| observer remedy | nothing | `spekk validate` before the commit |

Two of those were not weak wording but wrong instructions:

- `parseAllSpecs()` is an internal Go function. The skill named something an agent cannot run, so an agent following the step faithfully still validated nothing.
- The coach's re-coordinate list ran validation at step 4 and wrote frontmatter at step 5, so it checked the tree before the change it was meant to check.

Prompt text is kept to a minimum — one sentence on the observer, one comment line and a reordering on the coach.

## Docs

`docs/cli-reference.md` gains a short note on `depends-on`. It leads with the design reason rather than parser behaviour: the field holds one id because that is what controls the order work reaches builders. A chain releases assertions one at a time, and assertions with no link between them run in parallel. A set of prerequisites carries no such order, so the coordinator skill linearizes it into a chain.

## Check

```
$ spekk validate
validate: 36 specs, 193 assertions OK
```

`go test ./...` passes.

author: njhale
body:
A skill in a shared discovery directory was attributed to every client
documented as reading it, and build synthesized a clients[] row for any
name an observation referenced. One SKILL.md in ~/.claude/skills minted
rows for claude_code, cursor, opencode and vscode regardless of what was
installed.

Presence detection could not correct for it. A bare config directory
counted as an install, and hook-install creates ~/.claude itself; the
$PATH lookup answered "can the process that launched me run this", so a
scan from a scheduled task reported a different client set than the same
scan from a terminal.

Detect clients from paths that exist only when the client is on the
device: an install location, or state it writes by running (session
history, auth tokens, logs, state databases). Every signal is a glob, so
a literal and a version-segment pattern take the same code path. A
client earns a row when detection finds it or when it owns an MCP server
or plugin; skills never establish presence. Skill attribution intersects
with the clients found, falling back to the multi sentinel so no skill
leaves the manifest.

Restructure the package around the locations it reads rather than a
per-client interface, since the conventions are increasingly
client-neutral: skillDirs and skillTrees carry the clients that read each
path, sources pair a path with its decoder, and Client is reduced to
identity plus install evidence. Deletes the six-method Scanner interface,
whose implementations were almost entirely constants.

Also, finish up support for detecting antigravity configurations.

Fixes obot-platform/obot#7288
Addresses https://github.com/obot-platform/obot/issues/6751

author: raineorshine
body:
## What changed

Converts the package from CommonJS to native ES modules:

- **package.json**: `"type": "module"` and an `"exports"` map pointing `types` at the declaration file and `default` at `src/index.js`
- **src/index.js**: `import spawn from 'cross-spawn'` / `export default spawnPlease` instead of `require` / `module.exports`
- **Tests**: converted to ESM imports; `__dirname` is reconstructed from `import.meta.url`; chai is imported as a namespace (`import * as chai`) since chai 5+ is ESM-native with no default export
- **.eslintrc.json**: added `parserOptions` with `sourceType: "module"`
- **types**: regenerated declarations, now emitting `export default spawnPlease`

## Why

ESM is the standard module system; shipping ESM-only simplifies the package now that engines already require Node >= 22.

## Notes for reviewers

- ⚠️ **Breaking change**: CommonJS consumers can no longer `require('spawn-please')` — this warrants a major version bump (4.0.0) when publishing.
- The README already documents `import` usage, so no docs changes were needed.
- Verified locally on the upgraded toolchain: 11/11 mocha tests pass, `tsc` build clean, ESLint clean, plus an `import` smoke test of the entry point.

author: adhami3310
body:
## Rust deps

- **pyo3 0.28 → 0.29** (0.29.2). No source changes needed — `#[pymodule(gil_used = false)]`, `Bound`, and the `#[pyo3(signature = ...)]` attr all compile unchanged.
- **ruff git rev `9b03f2b2` → `fbe3e251`** (`ruff_python_formatter` / `ruff_python_parser`, crate versions 0.0.1 → 0.0.8).
- `cargo update` on the rest of the tree. Notable: `zip` 0.6.6 → 8.6.0, `wasm-bindgen` 0.2.118 → 0.2.127, `thiserror` 2.0.18 → 2.0.20, `zerocopy` 0.8.48 → 0.8.56. The lock shrinks a fair bit (dropped `wit-bindgen`/`wasm-*` and `serde_with`).

## CI

Re-pinned to the latest release SHAs:

- `actions/checkout` v6.0.2 → v7.0.1
- `actions/setup-python` v6.2.0 → v7.0.0
- `actions/attest` v4.1.0 → v4.2.2
- `astral-sh/setup-uv` v8.1.0 → v9.0.0
- `download-artifact` v8.0.1, `upload-artifact` v7.0.1 and `maturin-action` v1.51.0 were already current.

Two checks on the major bumps: setup-python v7 drops the `pip-install` input (unused here) and its "remove EOL Python versions" change only touched their own test workflows, so `python-version: "3.8"` still resolves. setup-uv v9 flips `prune-cache` to `false` by default — a cache-size change, not a behavior break.

I also regenerated the workflow from the maturin template to check for drift. maturin 1.14.1 emits a byte-identical template to 1.13.3 for this project, and our file already matches it apart from two deliberate local customizations, both preserved: the SHA pins (vs the template's floating `@v6`/`@v1` tags) and the omitted `UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN` env (we use PyPI trusted publishing via `id-token: write`). So the only change here is the header comment, now v1.14.1.

## Version: 0.5.2 → 0.5.4

Skipping 0.5.3 deliberately. The `v0.5.3` tag already exists on c6823b0, but that release never made it to PyPI — latest there is 0.5.2. Cargo.toml wasn't bumped in that commit, so the tagged build produced another 0.5.2 and PyPI would have rejected it as a duplicate. Reusing 0.5.3 now would collide with the existing tag, so 0.5.4 is the next clean number. Patch bump matches the precedent from #4, the previous deps bump.

## Test plan

- `cargo build` clean on pyo3 0.29 + the new ruff rev.
- `maturin develop` + smoke test: `format_string`, the `line_width=` kwarg, and `is_valid_syntax` all behave correctly.

author: seanpvera
body:
## What changed

- Model the Govee H612B Strip Light S as a flexible 75-zone strip and give it the strip-shaped editor it was missing.
- Replace the generic H60B0 segment treatment with an Uplighter Color Studio for its three named physical zones: Upper Ripple, Middle Ambient, and Lower Daily Illumination.
- Keep streamed H60B0 layouts alive without repeatedly toggling Razer mode, which could clear the current frame and produce visible flashes.
- Add a hardware-aware String Light Studio:
  - H70C1 uses 100 individually addressable LED beads.
  - H70C2 and H70C4 use 200 individually addressable LED beads.
  - H7020 and H7028 default to 15 outdoor bulbs.
  - H7021 uses 30 outdoor bulbs.
  - Expandable or unknown bulb strings retain an adjustable unit count.
- Classify H70B1/H70BC as curtain lights and present their 20 locally addressable vertical columns instead of masquerading as a one-dimensional string.
- Normalize legacy saved drafts to fixed hardware topologies, preserve active streamed layouts while a different draft is previewed, and update demo-workspace state handling.
- Add domain and protocol coverage for the new profiles, legacy-state normalization, applied-layout ownership, and 200-color streaming frames.
- Update the README with the hardware-specific editor behavior and troubleshooting guidance.

## Why

The previous editor treated too many physically different fixtures as the same short generic segment row. H612B lacked its strip profile, H60B0 exposed anonymous segments despite having three distinct lamps, Christmas strings were undercounted as 20 units, outdoor strings used inaccurate counts, and curtain lights were classified as strings. The stream keepalive could also re-enable Razer mode during routine refreshes, momentarily clearing an H60B0 frame.

## User impact

Each affected fixture now looks and edits like the hardware sitting in the room. Fixed products stay locked to their physical topology, individually addressable beads and bulbs can be selected by numbered position, legacy drafts repair themselves when opened, and routine stream refreshes preserve the visible uplighter frame.

## Validation

- `swiftc -frontend -parse` passed for every changed Swift source and test file.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- The current Xcode build and XCTest suite could not be rerun after the string-light additions because `/Applications/Xcode.app` is absent on this host and `xcode-select` currently points to Command Line Tools. CI should provide the full build result.

| channel | yes | yes | yes |
| description | no | **only source** | no |
| duration | no | no | **only source** |

Provenance was a single `varchar` that every pass overwrote, so whichever ran last claimed the whole row.

That model caused real loss. A bulk import relabelled **92 rows** that an earlier archive pass had recovered months before. No video data was lost — the titles and descriptions written by the earlier pass were intact — but the record of where they came from was gone, and the archive capture timestamps went with it, because the convention packed two facts into one string as `source:timestamp`.

The loss was undetectable after the fact. The obvious heuristic — "the importer never writes descriptions, so an importer-sourced row that has one must have come from elsewhere" — is wrong, since most such descriptions came from the original sync.

## What changed

Two append-only join tables, `video_recovery_sources` and `channel_recovery_sources`, holding one row per `(target, source)`.

- **The primary key is `(target, source)`, not a surrogate.** That is what makes *append, never overwrite* a constraint rather than a rule every caller has to remember: a source that runs twice refreshes its own row and leaves every other source's row untouched.
- **`source` and `source_detail` are separate columns**, so the packing that destroyed the timestamps has no equivalent here. The model refuses a `source` containing `:` outright rather than storing something that looks fine and is unqueryable.
- **`fields_written` is explicitly a hint**, not a guarantee — a pass that does not populate it still records that it touched the row.

`videos.recovery_source` and `recovered_at` are retained and the API still exposes them unchanged, so the detail endpoint needs no join per row. They become **derived**: a projection of the join table, recomputed rather than trusted from the caller. That is deliberately a second copy of a fact — the pattern that caused this — and the mitigation is that exactly one code path writes them. The projection still rebuilds the packed form for existing readers, and the column can be dropped once none depend on it.

The migration backfills existing single values, splitting the packed form into its two columns.

## Testing

The repository tests deliberately cross the boundary instead of asserting that the code called the functions it calls. The behaviour being protected is *what the database holds* after two sources touch the same row — an `ON CONFLICT` clause, a composite primary key and a derived column working together. A mocked session would have passed against the original defect.

Pure model validation (packed-source rejection, trimming, field bounds, immutability) needs no database and lives in unit tests.

## Also here

- **`docs/architecture/recovery-provenance.md`** — the model, what the denormalised column is for, and the three questions this deliberately does not answer. `data-model.md` and the generated schema reference point at it.
- **`gen_private_terms.py`** gains a third exclusion set for entities long used as fixture data, with the accepted blind spot stated in the file, plus two ASR mis-transcriptions that collide with a CSS colour and an English verb. Its summary line counted one of three sets, understating what is unguarded.

## Checks

`ruff` · `black --check` · `mypy --strict` · backend unit · backend integration · frontend tests + typecheck · `alembic check` (no model/migration drift) · `mkdocs build --strict` — all green locally.

Version **0.66.0**.

author: jrmoulckers
body:
Reported by the game-library adoption ([game-library#4](https://github.com/jrmoulckers/game-library/pull/4)), where `check-blank` produced **10 of 12** errcheck findings.

## The contradiction

`configs/golangci.yml` set `errcheck.check-blank: true`, banning `_ = f()` outright. `practices/go.md` says: *never discard an error with `_` unless the reason is stated in a comment beside it* — which explicitly **permits** the commented form. A consumer could not satisfy both.

**Verified against errcheck's source rather than accepting the report.** `checkAssignment` guards the blank check with `if call, ok := rhs[0].(*ast.CallExpr); ok` — so `_ = f()` is flagged and `err := f(); _ = err` is not, because the latter's RHS is an `*ast.Ident`. The option mandates a two-line spelling; it does not prevent the discard. That settles which side is wrong: the config was buying a rename, not a guarantee.

`check-type-assertions` **stays on**, deliberately not symmetrical — a failed assertion panics, and no comment makes that recoverable.

## practices/go.md

- States what a discard comment must contain, since review now carries the rule and "ignore error" records nothing reviewable.
- New section on sanitized error wrapping. `errorlint` flags `fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", ...)` and is usually right, but flattening the cause is sometimes deliberate sanitization — the reporter had six sites wrapping a sentinel while keeping a filesystem path unreachable via `errors.Is`/`As`. Guidance: if the cause is not sensitive use `%w: %w`; if it is, do not flatten inline — **sanitize at the boundary that knows the value is sensitive** and wrap normally, so the chain stays intact and the intent is visible to readers and the linter alike. Their in-package verification worked because they could read every caller; across a package boundary it does not.

## docs/adopting.md

Root placement and no-inheritance were already documented; these are new:

- **Validate shape, not just size.** `-f` catches a non-200 and `-s` catches truncation — neither catches a **200 carrying the wrong body**. Assert top-level `version:` and `linters:`.
- **Stage, validate, move.** Fetching straight to `.golangci.yml` leaves a corrupt file exactly where the linter reads it. Write to a temp file and `mv` only after every check passes.
- **Gitignore the fetched path** — makes "do not vendor" structural rather than advisory.
- **Measured adoption cost:** ~20 findings per 30 previously unlinted files, and why fixing beats `//nolint`.

## New test

**Nothing in this repo tested the Go config at all** — the same gap shape as no test ever running ESLint before #46. There is no Go toolchain here, so `golangci-lint config verify` belongs in a consumer (it passed there against v2.12.2, all ten linters resolving). `scripts/test/go-config.test.mjs` guards the two classes a consumer *cannot* catch for us:

1. The published file failing the validation we instruct every consumer to run — that break is ours, and it fails their pipeline closed.
2. A setting drifting back into contradicting `go.md`. Pinned bidirectionally: deleting the practice's carve-out sentence also fails.

All four guards mutation-tested (`check-blank` to true, `check-type-assertions` to false, `version:` removed, practice sentence reworded — each fails exactly one). My first attempt at the fourth silently no-oped because a stray comma made PowerShell bind an array; redone. Assertions match whitespace-normalized source, never exact lines, since a source-reading guard is the thing most likely to be silently disarmed by a formatter change.

## Verification

`npm test` **118/118** (was 114), `format:check` clean, coverage 59/66 unchanged, citations 472 all-exist, no changes under `principles/` or `docs/ratification/`.

author: h2oking89
body:
## Summary

Completes the maintainability and scalability roadmap through Milestone 6. The branch replaces global ViewModel dependency state with application-owned construction, makes template editing route-restorable, separates stateful routes from stateless screens, decomposes large UI surfaces, adds CI and release safeguards, and documents the resulting architecture.

## Changes

### Correctness and ownership
- Made full-backup restore atomic: resolved templates, optional technician profile, and active-template selection are persisted in one `DataStore.updateData` transaction.
- Removed obsolete template APIs and uncollected error events from `SettingsViewModel`.
- Added `Routes.TemplateEditor(templateId)` and a destination-scoped `TemplateEditorViewModel` backed by `SavedStateHandle`.
- Introduced `AppContainer` as the process-scoped owner of `SettingsStore`, resource access, updater access, import/export repository, and package-manager access.
- Made `AppViewModelProvider` a stateless adapter over `AppContainer`; removed static dependency fields and global reset hooks.

### UI architecture and decomposition
- Added Route/Screen boundaries for Customer Intake, Settings, Import, Export, Template List, and Template Editor.
- Moved ViewModel access, state collection, effects, navigation, and Android I/O to routes; screens now render explicit state and callbacks.
- Split Customer Intake, settings, import/export, template UI, QR-sheet content, and reusable neon components into focused files.
- Added focused Compose coverage for extracted sections and stateless screens.

### Tooling, CI, and documentation
- Added PR/default-branch emulator smoke coverage and scheduled/manual full instrumentation coverage with report uploads.
- Hardened Android workflow credentials and pinned checkout, setup-java, and emulator-runner actions to commit SHAs.
- Added weekly Dependabot updates for Gradle and GitHub Actions.
- Hardened release automation by validating tag/version alignment and changelog presence before signing, then running unit tests, Ktlint, Detekt, and lint.
- Configured Detekt for Compose function naming and the `import_pkg` convention; regenerated the baseline from 195 to 72 remaining findings.
- Added architecture, dependency-update, and troubleshooting guides; updated the roadmap and release guide.

## Validation

- `./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest :app:compileDebugAndroidTestKotlin :app:ktlintCheck :app:detekt :app:lintDebug :app:assembleDebug`
- `git diff --check`
- Workflow YAML and embedded Bash parsed locally.
- Verified the corrected instrumentation class filter on SM-S938U / API 36: `TemplateEditorScreenTest` completed 33/33 tests with UTP exit code `0`.
- Direct, fresh-process device batches passed 94/94 instrumentation tests (18 + 28 + 33 + 15); batching avoids Samsung process-freezer false failures seen in a monolithic run.

## Review Notes

No functional blockers found in the persistence, navigation, route/screen, DI, or lifecycle changes. The removed `AppViewModelProvider.resetForTesting()` calls are intentional because the provider no longer has static mutable dependencies.

The new report-upload steps retain the repository's existing `actions/upload-artifact@v4` tag usage. This PR pins the three actions requested for the Android workflow (`checkout`, `setup-java`, and `android-emulator-runner`); consider pinning `upload-artifact` in a follow-up if the repository adopts an all-actions SHA-pinning policy.

## Risk and Rollout

This is a broad structural refactor that preserves public workflows while tightening state ownership. The primary operational risk is first-run behavior of the new GitHub-hosted emulator jobs; they are locally syntax-validated and use test classes verified on a physical device, but their hosted runner execution will be established by this PR's CI run.

author: kforbus3
body:
Reported from a real decommission: the v1.5.0 teardown removed the `fleet` accounts and **left the VPN up and operational**. Two independent bugs, one per end — which is why the tunnel wasn't merely configured but still handshaking.

## 1. The teardown never touched the overlay (mine, v1.5.0)

`hostTeardownScript` removed the sudoers grant, both accounts, the CA trust, the principal files and the sshd drop-in — and left the WireGuard interface up and enabled at boot. A host deleted from Fleet kept a live tunnel onto the fleet's network with nothing on it that Fleet managed or audited.

`scripts/fleet-unenroll.sh` retired the transport from its first commit, and `docs/host-enrollment-guide.md` listed it in the table for *both* paths. So the gap existed only in the generated script, and only if you read it.

The teardown now embeds the host's transport retire script — `wgTeardownScript`, or the overlay's `RetireHostScript()` for a certificate overlay — and runs it **last**, after the accounts are gone. Last for two reasons: it's the transport Fleet arrived over, so it can't come down while the session is using it (hence it must be on the detached side), and running it after the accounts means the privileged account is already removed even if the transport teardown stalls. An overlay this deployment can't provision now warns loudly in `/var/log/fleet-unenroll.log` instead of being silently skipped.

## 2. The jump-host half had never run at all (pre-existing)

`CleanupHostOverlay` dialed the jump host like this:

```go
jumpClient, err := s.gw.DialDirect(ctx, uuid.New().String(), jumpAddr, jumpPort, s.cfg.JumpUser)
```

`DialDirect` resolves that session id against the identity vault. A UUID generated on the spot has no credential there, by construction — so every call returned `no live credential for session` before a packet was sent. It's the only one of the five `DialDirect` call sites that doesn't pass a real session id; the other four are user-session flows.

It's invoked from a goroutine that only logs a warning, so nothing ever surfaced. **Every host deleted from Fleet, in any version carrying this code, kept its peer on the hub.** Enrollment retires stale claims inline when an overlay address is reissued, so peers self-healed as addresses got reused — which is why this never looked like a bug.

Fixed with a new `Gateway.DialJumpSystem`: a short-lived system certificate carrying the fleet-wide principal, which is what the jump host trusts and what every other background path already uses.

> **If you have deleted hosts before upgrading, their peers are still on the jump host.** They self-heal as addresses are reused; to clear them sooner, remove the peers there directly.

## 3. A requested teardown now reports both ends

With teardown ticked, peer retirement runs synchronously and a failure is named in the UI next to an unreachable host. "Decommission this host" is a claim about both ends. Deleting *without* teardown keeps the background best-effort behaviour unchanged.

## Tests

Both regression tests were **verified to fail against the shipped code** before being committed:

- `TestTeardownRetiresTheOverlay` — the generated script must bring the tunnel down, disable the boot unit, delete the interface and set the config aside, for WireGuard and for a cert overlay (via a stub provisioner), and must warn when the overlay is unavailable.
- `TestTeardownPathsDoNotDrift` — walks an artifact list against **both** the generated script and `scripts/fleet-unenroll.sh`. The two implementations diverged the moment the second was written; this is the guard that would have caught it. The original cross-check only compared against `caTrustScript`, which doesn't install WireGuard — the hole was exactly where the bug was.
- `TestCleanupHostOverlayDoesNotUseASessionCredential` — distinguishes the failure *site*: the broken path fails in the vault lookup, the fixed one reaches the issuer.

`go build`, `go vet`, `go test ./...`, `tsc --noEmit` and the frontend suite all pass.

author: fedcourtsai-dev[bot]
body:
Routine catch-up so **staging keeps containing main**, opened by the scheduled
`sync-staging` workflow. See that workflow header for why this runs on a
schedule rather than at promotion time.

main is **14** commit(s) ahead: the deterministic writers and the bot
lanes commit there directly and never ride staging.

**Merge with a merge commit, never a squash** — the promotion gate asserts that
main is an ancestor of staging, and a squash would rewrite the merged history
and break that. Auto-merge is armed to do exactly that once `gate` and `paths`
pass; if it never fires, this merge conflicts and needs resolving here.

author: n-e-o-w-u-l-f
body:
## Summary

Introduces a system-native release boundary for devkit-wulf. Shared environment intent may remain common across platforms, but release-facing installer entrypoints, executable formats, package managers, privilege handling and host mutation are bound to an explicit operating-system/domain family.

## Installer families

Adds separate release-facing entrypoints for:

- Windows native: `installers/windows/devkit-wulf.ps1`
- Linux native: `installers/linux/devkit-wulf.sh`
- WSL2 Linux: `installers/wsl/devkit-wulf.sh`
- macOS: `installers/macos/devkit-wulf.sh`
- BSD: `installers/bsd/devkit-wulf.sh`
- Solaris/illumos: `installers/solaris/devkit-wulf.sh`
- AIX: `installers/aix/devkit-wulf.sh`

Each entrypoint proves its host family/domain before delegating to the existing internal orchestration core. Native Linux explicitly rejects WSL; the WSL entrypoint requires WSL markers.

## Release artifact policy

`manifests/installer-families.json` makes the following invariants machine-readable:

- no universal cross-OS release artifact;
- Windows `.exe`/`.msi` formats are Windows-only;
- Linux/WSL/macOS/BSD/Solaris/AIX release formats remain system-specific;
- shared internal orchestration code is allowed, but release-facing entrypoints remain system-native;
- WSL runs the Linux payload inside the distribution while Windows-side WSL provisioning remains a separate PowerShell/system-change contract.

## Shared environment contracts

Adds `environments/` as the future root for platform-neutral/version-specific environment intent. Shared contracts describe WHAT should exist after installation; system-native adapters describe HOW to achieve it.

The architecture documentation uses Python 3.12 as the concrete model:

```text
environments/python/3.12.json
installers/windows/environments/python-3.12.ps1
installers/linux/environments/python-3.12.sh
installers/macos/environments/python-3.12.sh
```

The version/components/verification policy can be shared while trusted sources, installer formats, package managers, privilege, PATH, conflicts and uninstall ownership remain host-specific.

## CI / gates

Adds `tests/validate_installer_families.py` and `.github/workflows/installer-families.yml` to enforce:

- exact installer family set;
- unique system-native entrypoints;
- no Windows executable formats leaking into non-Windows families;
- explicit Linux-vs-WSL separation;
- POSIX syntax/host guards;
- Windows PowerShell parser validity;
- wrong-family entrypoints fail closed on Linux.

All POSIX release entrypoints are executable (`100755`) and avoid GNU-specific `dirname --` / `cd --` assumptions.

## Migration boundary

Existing `bin/` and `lib/` logic remains in place as an internal migration core. This PR does not remove working adapters, change environment support states, or promote any platform/environment combination. New installer work should target the system-native tree; existing code can migrate incrementally without weakening security gates.

Continuation of issue #2.
